subtitle: Frequently asked questions about the Internet for newcomers.

tldr.problem: New Internet users have common questions about the Internet, its structure, and how to use it effectively.
tldr.mechanism: This FYI document collects the most frequently asked questions from new users and provides straightforward answers about Internet basics, protocols, services, and organizations.
tldr.outcome: Newcomers gain practical knowledge about the Internet and where to find further information. It was updated by RFC 1325.

today: RFC 1206 is an Informational document and has been obsoleted by RFC 1325. It represents early efforts to document frequently asked questions about the Internet for newcomers joining the network in 1991.

sections.title: What is the Internet
sections.content:
The Internet is a large collection of interconnected networks that all run the TCP/IP protocol suite. It started with the ARPANET but now includes universities, research institutions, government facilities, and many corporations worldwide. Users on any Internet network can reach users and services on any other network using TCP/IP protocols.

When you join the Internet, you gain access to three main capabilities: file transfer between computers, remote login (TELNET) to work interactively on distant machines, and electronic mail to communicate with users on the Internet and on many non-Internet networks via mail gateways.
sections.eli5: The Internet is like a giant library where all the computers are connected. You can borrow files from other computers, visit other machines far away, or send messages to other people.

sections.title: TCP/IP and the Domain Name System
sections.content:
TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) is a family of over 100 protocols used to connect computers and equipment into networks. The main protocols include TCP and IP for network communication, SMTP for mail transfer, FTP for file transfer, and TELNET for remote login. All Internet hosts use TCP/IP, and the Internet Activities Board (IAB) regularly publishes a standard document describing the state of each protocol.

The Domain Name System (DNS) is a hierarchical, distributed method for organizing the Internet's name space. Instead of relying on a single central file that maps host names to addresses, the DNS distributes this information across many servers organized by domain. A Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) includes the host name plus all higher-level domain names up to the root; for example, PARIS.NISC.SRI.COM is a FQDN where each dot represents a level in the domain hierarchy.
sections.eli5: TCP/IP is the common language that all computers use to talk to each other. DNS is like a phonebook that translates human-friendly names (like PARIS.NISC.SRI.COM) into computer addresses so your messages get to the right place.

sections.title: RFCs and Internet Documentation
sections.content:
Requests for Comments (RFCs) are the working notes of the Internet research and development community. They may cover anything from network protocols to meeting reports or policy studies. While RFCs are not formally refereed, they do receive technical review. Most standards are published as RFCs, but not all RFCs specify standards. Once published with an RFC number, a document is never revised with the same number; if a protocol improves, a new RFC is issued. The IAB Official Protocol Standards memo is the authoritative reference for determining the correct RFC for the current specification of each protocol.

RFCs can be obtained via FTP from NIC.DDN.MIL or NIS.NSF.NET using anonymous login, or through automatic mail service. The NIC maintains an online index of all RFCs. Internet Drafts are working documents of the IETF, valid for six months, and should not be cited as standards or archived materials.
sections.eli5: RFCs are like official notebooks where people write down how Internet protocols work. They are public and numbered so you can always find the right one. Internet Drafts are newer, temporary papers that people are still working on.

sections.title: Internet Organizations and Management
sections.content:
The Internet Activities Board (IAB) is the coordinating committee for Internet design, engineering, and management. It sets Internet standards, manages RFC publication, reviews the IETF and IRTF, performs strategic planning, and serves as an international technical representative. The IAB has two main task forces: the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), which handles near-term engineering problems, and the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), which addresses long-term research problems.

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) coordinates the assignment of protocol parameters like op-codes, type fields, and port numbers. The Network Information Center (NIC) provides network information services and user assistance. The DDN NIC at SRI International serves as the primary repository for RFCs and Internet Drafts and maintains the WHOIS database of network users, hosts, and domains.
sections.eli5: The IAB is the main committee that makes decisions about the Internet. The IETF solves practical problems that engineers face right now, while the IRTF studies long-term research questions. IANA keeps track of all the numbers and codes used by protocols, and the NIC is like an information center where you can look up facts about Internet computers and people.

sections.title: Internet Services and Tools
sections.content:
Electronic mail is a primary Internet service, with several directories available to help find addresses, including the WHOIS database at the DDN NIC, the PSI White Pages, and the Knowbot Information Service. To use WHOIS, TELNET to NIC.DDN.MIL and type 'whois' at the prompt.

Anonymous FTP is a standard way to access public files on Internet computers; you log in with username 'anonymous' and use your email address as the password. Many sites distribute software and information this way. TELNET is the protocol for remote login, letting you connect to a distant computer as if your terminal were directly connected; most TELNET services require an account on the remote host, though some provide public services like directory access.

Usenet and Netnews are a distributed bulletin board system that many Internet computers participate in, used for discussion groups. Mailing lists are aliases with multiple destinations, created to discuss specific topics; most large lists have a '-request' address for administrative messages like joining or leaving.
sections.eli5: Email is how you send messages. WHOIS is like a phonebook where you can look up people. Anonymous FTP lets you copy files from other computers. TELNET lets you work on another computer far away. Usenet is a public bulletin board where people post messages about topics they care about.
